claim: Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a facultative intracellular pathogen that uses its type 3 secretion system 2 (T3SS2) to invade and replicate inside host cells.
source: Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a facultative intracellular pathogen that uses its type 3 secretion system 2 (T3SS2) to invade and replicate inside host cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about V. parahaemolyticus.

claim: VPA0226, a constitutively secreted lipase, is required for escape of V. parahaemolyticus from host cells.
source: Using a combination of molecular tools, we found that VPA0226, a constitutively secreted lipase, is required for escape of V. parahaemolyticus from the host cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: VPA0226 must be delivered into the host cytoplasm to function.
source: This lipase must be delivered into the host cytoplasm where it preferentially uses fatty acids associated with innate immune response to esterify cholesterol, weakening the plasma membrane and allowing egress of the bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations showing VPA0226 activity only in invaded cells.

claim: VPA0226 preferentially uses fatty acids associated with innate immune response to esterify cholesterol.
source: This lipase must be delivered into the host cytoplasm where it preferentially uses fatty acids associated with innate immune response to esterify cholesterol, weakening the plasma membrane and allowing egress of the bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic data showing increased cholesteryl esters with specific PUFAs (20:3, 20:4, 20:5, 22:6).

claim: Esterification of cholesterol by VPA0226 weakens the plasma membrane and allows bacterial egress.
source: This lipase must be delivered into the host cytoplasm where it preferentially uses fatty acids associated with innate immune response to esterify cholesterol, weakening the plasma membrane and allowing egress of the bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by data showing membrane permeability changes, susceptibility to mechanical stress, and rescue experiments with cholesterol.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus is a Gram-negative bacterium that resides in warm estuarine environments.
source: For example, the facultative intracellular pathogen Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a Gram-negative bacterium that resides in warm estuarine environments with some strains acquiring virulence factors that can cause illness, even death in animals including shrimp and humans (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Some strains of V. parahaemolyticus acquire virulence factors that can cause illness and death in animals including shrimp and humans.
source: For example, the facultative intracellular pathogen Vibrio parahaemolyticus is a Gram-negative bacterium that resides in warm estuarine environments with some strains acquiring virulence factors that can cause illness, even death in animals including shrimp and humans (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus can cause acute gastroenteritis due to consumption of contaminated, undercooked seafood.
source: This pathogen can cause acute gastroenteritis due to the consumption of contaminated, undercooked seafood and possibly septicemia when infecting open wounds (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus can possibly cause septicemia when infecting open wounds.
source: This pathogen can cause acute gastroenteritis due to the consumption of contaminated, undercooked seafood and possibly septicemia when infecting open wounds (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Wang et al., 2015 and includes the qualifier 'possibly'.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus contains hemolysins secreted via T2SS and two Type 3 Secretion Systems (T3SS1 and T3SS2).
source: V. parahaemolyticus contains a number of virulence factors, including hemolysins secreted via T2SS (Type 2 Secretion System) and two Type 3 Secretion Systems (T3SS1 and T3SS2) (Makino et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Makino et al., 2003.

claim: T2SS is primarily involved in exporting folded proteins from the periplasm of most Gram-negative bacteria into extracellular environment.
source: T2SS is primarily involved in exporting folded proteins from the periplasm of most Gram-negative bacteria into extracellular environment and is a part of the widely conserved general secretory (Sec) pathway (Korotkov et al., 2012; Douzi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Korotkov et al., 2012 and Douzi et al., 2012.

claim: T2SS is a part of the widely conserved general secretory (Sec) pathway.
source: T2SS is primarily involved in exporting folded proteins from the periplasm of most Gram-negative bacteria into extracellular environment and is a part of the widely conserved general secretory (Sec) pathway (Korotkov et al., 2012; Douzi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Korotkov et al., 2012 and Douzi et al., 2012.

claim: T2SS is a specialized multicomponent assembly that consists of four major components: an outer membrane secretin, an inner membrane channel, the pseudopilus and an ATPase.
source: T2SS is a specialized multicomponent assembly that consists of four major components: an outer membrane secretin, an inner membrane channel, the pseudopilus and an ATPase (Douzi et al., 2012; Silva et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Douzi et al., 2012 and Silva et al., 2020.

claim: T2SS secreted protein repertoire includes various carbohydrate, lipid and protein hydrolyzing enzymes, pore-forming toxins, phosphatases, nucleases, etc.
source: T2SS secreted protein repertoire includes various carbohydrate, lipid and protein hydrolyzing enzymes, pore-forming toxins, phosphatases, nucleases, etc. that are implicated in plant, animal and human pathogenesis and widely present in both intracellular and extracellular pathogens (Nivaskumar and Francetic, 2014; Cianciotto and White, 2017; Cianciotto, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Nivaskumar and Francetic, 2014; Cianciotto and White, 2017; Cianciotto, 2005.

claim: T2SS secreted proteins are implicated in plant, animal and human pathogenesis and widely present in both intracellular and extracellular pathogens.
source: T2SS secreted protein repertoire includes various carbohydrate, lipid and protein hydrolyzing enzymes, pore-forming toxins, phosphatases, nucleases, etc. that are implicated in plant, animal and human pathogenesis and widely present in both intracellular and extracellular pathogens (Nivaskumar and Francetic, 2014; Cianciotto and White, 2017; Cianciotto, 2005).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Nivaskumar and Francetic, 2014; Cianciotto and White, 2017; Cianciotto, 2005.

claim: In Vibrio species, hemolysins including TDH, TRH and the cholera toxin are secreted via the T2SS.
source: In Vibrio species, hemolysins including TDH (Thermostable Direct Hemolysin), TRH (TDH-related Hemolysin) and the cholera toxin are known to be secreted via the T2SS (Matsuda et al., 2019; Sikora, 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Matsuda et al., 2019 and Sikora, 2013.

claim: T3SS1 is associated with all strains of V. parahaemolyticus.
source: Previous studies have shown that the more ancient T3SS1 is associated with all strains of V. parahaemolyticus, whereas T3SS2, a more recent acquisition, correlates with clinical isolates and disease in humans (Makino et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Makino et al., 2003.

claim: T3SS2 is a more recent acquisition that correlates with clinical isolates and disease in humans.
source: Previous studies have shown that the more ancient T3SS1 is associated with all strains of V. parahaemolyticus, whereas T3SS2, a more recent acquisition, correlates with clinical isolates and disease in humans (Makino et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Makino et al., 2003.

claim: CAB2 is a strain derived from the clinical isolate RIMD2210633 that is deleted for hemolysins and mutated for expression of the T3SS1.
source: Herein, to study T3SS2, we utilize CAB2, a strain derived from the clinical isolate RIMD2210633 that is deleted for hemolysins and mutated for expression of the T3SS1 (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: T3SS2 encodes a needle-like apparatus and effectors that mediate an invasive infection resulting in host cell death.
source: The T3SS2, found on a pathogenicity island encodes a needle-like apparatus and effectors that mediate an invasive infection resulting in host cell death (Zhang and Orth, 2013; de Souza Santos and Orth, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Zhang and Orth, 2013 and de Souza Santos and Orth, 2014.

claim: T3SS2 translocates the effector VopC, a deamidase, to mediate membrane ruffling and uptake of V. parahaemolyticus by nonphagocytic cells.
source: T3SS2 translocates the effector VopC, a deamidase, to mediate membrane ruffling and uptake of V. parahaemolyticus by nonphagocytic cells (Zhang et al., 2012; de Souza Santos and Orth, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Zhang et al., 2012 and de Souza Santos and Orth, 2014.

claim: Once inside, V. parahaemolyticus escapes from an acidified endocytic compartment and proceeds to replicate in the cytoplasm of the host cell, reaching counts of 200–300 bacteria per host cell.
source: Once inside, V. parahaemolyticus escapes from an acidified endocytic compartment and proceeds to replicate in the cytoplasm of the host cell, reaching counts of 200–300 bacteria per host cell (de Souza Santos and Orth, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to de Souza Santos and Orth, 2014.

claim: The acetyltransferase VopA blocks MAPK signaling.
source: Other translocated effectors have been shown to manipulate host cell signaling, including the acetyltransferase VopA that blocks MAPK signaling and the actin assembly factor VopL that blocks production of reactive oxygen species (Trosky et al., 2004; Liverman et al., 2007; de Souza Santos et al., 2017; Trosky et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Trosky et al., 2004; Liverman et al., 2007; de Souza Santos et al., 2017; Trosky et al., 2007.

claim: The actin assembly factor VopL blocks production of reactive oxygen species.
source: Other translocated effectors have been shown to manipulate host cell signaling, including the acetyltransferase VopA that blocks MAPK signaling and the actin assembly factor VopL that blocks production of reactive oxygen species (Trosky et al., 2004; Liverman et al., 2007; de Souza Santos et al., 2017; Trosky et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Trosky et al., 2004; Liverman et al., 2007; de Souza Santos et al., 2017; Trosky et al., 2007.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus ultimately escapes from its replicative niche to infect other cells.
source: V. parahaemolyticus ultimately escapes from this protective replicative niche to infect other cells (de Souza Santos and Orth, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to de Souza Santos and Orth, 2014.

claim: About a dozen T3SS2 effectors are thought to be delivered to the host cell.
source: In total, about a dozen T3SS2 effectors are thought to be delivered to the host cell, some with known molecular functions but with exception of the aforementioned effectors, understudied for their role in bacterial intracellular survival (De Souza Santos and Orth, 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to De Souza Santos and Orth, 2019.

claim: After bioinformatic perusal of the T3SS2 pathogenicity island, there appeared to be no obvious candidate effector that would mediate the escape of V. parahaemolyticus from the endocytic compartment or the host cell.
source: After bioinformatic perusal of this pathogenicity island, there appeared to be no obvious candidate effector that would mediate the escape of V. parahaemolyticus from the endocytic compartment or the host cell.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Pathogens use various mechanisms for egress, including programmed cell death, non-lytic exit of host cells and manipulation of host-cell-derived membranes.
source: Pathogens use various mechanisms for egress, including programmed cell death, non-lytic exit of host cells and manipulation of host-cell-derived membranes (Hybiske and Stephens, 2015; Flieger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hybiske and Stephens, 2015 and Flieger et al., 2018.

claim: Three forms of programmed cell death include both non-lytic (apoptosis) and lytic pathways (pyroptosis and necroptosis).
source: Three forms of programmed cell death that include both non-lytic (apoptosis) and lytic pathways (pyroptosis and necroptosis) are observed in pathogen egress.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about programmed cell death.

claim: M. tuberculosis and Leishmania species use apoptosis for pathogen egress.
source: For pathogen egress via apoptosis as seen with M. tuberculosis and Leishmania species, the invaded host cells are programmed to die without inducing inflammation. Thus, the pathogens cause less damage to the host leading to their dissemination within apoptotic bodies only to be engulfed by scavenging macrophages (Martin et al., 2012; van Zandbergen et al., 2004; Peters et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Martin et al., 2012; van Zandbergen et al., 2004; Peters et al., 2008.

claim: Pyroptosis is induced by gasdermin in a caspase-dependent pathway.
source: Pyroptosis, induced by gasdermin in a caspase-dependent pathway, involves formation of pores in the plasma membrane and is used as an exit mechanism by Francisella, Legionella, Shigella, Salmonella and Listeria (Hybiske and Stephens, 2008; Traven and Naderer, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hybiske and Stephens, 2008 and Traven and Naderer, 2014.

claim: Pyroptosis involves formation of pores in the plasma membrane and is used as an exit mechanism by Francisella, Legionella, Shigella, Salmonella and Listeria.
source: Pyroptosis, induced by gasdermin in a caspase-dependent pathway, involves formation of pores in the plasma membrane and is used as an exit mechanism by Francisella, Legionella, Shigella, Salmonella and Listeria (Hybiske and Stephens, 2008; Traven and Naderer, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hybiske and Stephens, 2008 and Traven and Naderer, 2014.

claim: Necroptosis is a programmed necrosis induced by the receptor-interacting protein kinase 3 (RIP3/RIPK3) and the mixed lineage kinase domain like pseudokinase (MLKL) signaling pathway.
source: Necroptosis, a programmed necrosis that is induced by the receptor-interacting protein kinase 3 (RIP3/RIPK3) and the mixed lineage kinase domain like pseudokinase (MLKL) signaling pathway, is observed for dissemination of Salmonella and Mycobacterium species (Lindgren et al., 1996; Dallenga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Lindgren et al., 1996 and Dallenga et al., 2017.

claim: Necroptosis is observed for dissemination of Salmonella and Mycobacterium species.
source: Necroptosis, a programmed necrosis that is induced by the receptor-interacting protein kinase 3 (RIP3/RIPK3) and the mixed lineage kinase domain like pseudokinase (MLKL) signaling pathway, is observed for dissemination of Salmonella and Mycobacterium species (Lindgren et al., 1996; Dallenga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Lindgren et al., 1996 and Dallenga et al., 2017.

claim: Many intracellular pathogens such as Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Mycobacterium, Shigella, Listeria and Legionella exit host cells by membrane protrusion, budding, exocytosis and expulsion.
source: Following non-lysing pathways, many intracellular pathogens such as Chlamydia, Rickettsia, Mycobacterium, Shigella, Listeria and Legionella exit host cells by membrane protrusion, budding, exocytosis and expulsion (Hybiske and Stephens, 2015; Flieger et al., 2018; Friedrich et al., 2012)
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hybiske and Stephens, 2015; Flieger et al., 2018; Friedrich et al., 2012.

claim: Parasites such as Trypanosoma, Plasmodium and Toxoplasma gondi use active host cell lysis mediated by proteases and lipases as exit strategy.
source: Parasites such as Trypanosoma, Plasmodium and Toxoplasma gondi use active host cell lysis mediated by proteases and lipases as exit strategy (Hybiske and Stephens, 2015; Pszenny et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Hybiske and Stephens, 2015 and Pszenny et al., 2016.

claim: VPA0226 is necessary for egress of V. parahaemolyticus from its host cell initially invaded in a T3SS2-mediated mechanism.
source: We show that the lipase, VPA0226 is necessary for egress of V. parahaemolyticus from its host cell initially invaded in a T3SS2-mediated mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by gentamicin protection assays.

claim: VPA0226 is not secreted by the T3SS2, but rather it is constitutively secreted by the type two secretion system.
source: However, VPA0226 is not secreted by the T3SS2, but rather it is constitutively secreted by the type two secretion system.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by secretion assays with various strains.

claim: Cytoplasmic VPA0226, but not its catalytically inactive forms (VPA0226-H/A or VPA0226-S/A), esterifies cholesterol using host polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA).
source: Using lipidomic studies we found that, unlike other bacterial lipases, cytoplasmic VPA0226, but not its catalytically inactive forms (VPA0226-H/A or VPA0226-S/A), esterifies cholesterol using host polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), specifically those implicated in immune signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by lipidomic analysis.

claim: VPA0226 specifically uses PUFAs implicated in immune signaling to esterify cholesterol.
source: Using lipidomic studies we found that, unlike other bacterial lipases, cytoplasmic VPA0226, but not its catalytically inactive forms (VPA0226-H/A or VPA0226-S/A), esterifies cholesterol using host polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), specifically those implicated in immune signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the Results section and supported by lipidomic analysis showing increased CE(20:3), CE(20:4), CE(20:5) and CE(22:6).

claim: VPA0226 has approximately 16% sequence identity with SseJ.
source: Using SseJ as a probe in a bioinformatic search of the V. parahaemolyticus genome, we identified a lipase (VPA0226) with approximately 16% sequence identity and conservation of catalytic residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VPA0226 has conservation of catalytic residues with SseJ.
source: Using SseJ as a probe in a bioinformatic search of the V. parahaemolyticus genome, we identified a lipase (VPA0226) with approximately 16% sequence identity and conservation of catalytic residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VPA0226 has lipase activity as demonstrated in vitro.
source: Previously, in vitro studies demonstrated that VPA0226 has lipase activity and structural studies on a related Vibrio vulnificus lipase revealed a chloride-dependent catalytic diad (Wan et al., 2019; Shinoda et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Wan et al., 2019 and Shinoda et al., 1991.

claim: VPA0226 contains a classic catalytic triad of Ser-His-Asp.
source: However, analysis of VPA0226 reveals a more classic catalytic triad of Ser-His-Asp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus CAB2 containing a functional T3SS2 can efficiently invade, replicate, and escape from the host cell.
source: We observed that the V. parahaemolyticus CAB2 containing a functional T3SS2 can efficiently invade, replicate (indicated by the increase in colony-forming units (CFU)), and escape from the host cell (indicated by the after-peak decrease in CFU due to exposure of egressed bacteria to gentamicin) (Figure 1A, black bars).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CAB2Δvpa0226 results in cells that have increasing amounts of bacteria with no significant decrease for up to 7 hr post-gentamicin treatment, indicating the inability of these bacteria to escape from an invaded cell.
source: By contrast, a CAB2 strain deleted for vpa0226 (CAB2Δvpa0226) results in cells that have increasing amounts of bacteria with no significant decrease for up to 7 hr post-gentamicin treatment (PGT), indicating the inability of these bacteria to escape from an invaded cell (Figure 1A, green bars).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In-trans complementation with a wildtype copy of VPA0226 allowed for bacterial escape.
source: While in-trans complementation with a wildtype copy of VPA0226 allowed for bacterial escape, the catalytically inactive form of VPA0226 did not allow for egress of V. parahaemolyticus from the host cell. (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The catalytically inactive form of VPA0226 did not allow for egress of V. parahaemolyticus from the host cell.
source: While in-trans complementation with a wildtype copy of VPA0226 allowed for bacterial escape, the catalytically inactive form of VPA0226 did not allow for egress of V. parahaemolyticus from the host cell. (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: VPA0226 is constitutively secreted from V. parahaemolyticus strains CAB2, CAB3, and CAB4.
source: To our surprise, with the exception of the CAB2Δvpa0226 strain, we observed VPA0226 to be constitutively secreted from all of these V. parahaemolyticus strains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: VPA0226 contains a signal peptide at its N-terminus similar to those found for enzymes that are secreted out of the type two secretion system.
source: Further bioinformatic analysis using SignalP5.0 revealed that VPA0226 contained a signal peptide at its N-terminus similar to those found for enzymes that are secreted out of the type two secretion system (Banerji et al., 2005; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a citation to Banerji et al., 2005 and supported by SignalP prediction shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: VPA0226 is secreted by CAB2 and CAB2ΔepsD+EpsD, but not by CAB2Δvpa0226 or CAB2ΔepsD.
source: We observed that VPA0226 is secreted by CAB2 and CAB2ΔepsD+EpsD, but not by CAB2Δvpa0226 or CAB2ΔepsD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the expression level of VPA0226 in CAB2ΔepsD compared to CAB2.
source: As we did not observe VPA0226 in the pellet fraction of CAB2ΔepsD, we performed qPCR analysis to confirm the expression of VPA0226 in CAB2ΔepsD strain and observed a significant reduction in the expression level of VPA0226 in CAB2ΔepsD compared to CAB2 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VPA0226 is secreted by the type two secretion system.
source: Taken together, these above results demonstrate that VPA0226 is secreted by the type two secretion system (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: Cells expressing VPA0226-GFP died within 24 hr.
source: To test this hypothesis, we transiently transfected VPA0226 tagged with GFP (VPA0226-GFP) into HeLa cells and observed that cells expressing VPA0226-GFP died within 24 hr (data not shown); however, at an earlier time point (14 hr), the transfected cells were viable.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from transfection experiments.

claim: VPA0226-GFP was not localized to the plasma membrane but to an intracellular membrane compartment.
source: Somewhat perplexing, VPA0226-GFP was not localized to the plasma membrane but to an intracellular membrane compartment (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: VPA0226 associates with the mitochondria.
source: The only markers co-staining with VPA0226 were ACAT1 and COXIV, indicating that VPA0226 associates with the mitochondria (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images showing colocalization with mitochondrial markers.

claim: Cells transfected with the wildtype VPA0226 display fragmented mitochondria.
source: In addition, while mitochondria of cells mock-transfected or transfected with the catalytically inactive VPA0226 (VPA0226-H/A) show normal cell morphology, cells transfected with the wildtype VPA0226 display fragmented mitochondria (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images.

claim: Host cells invaded with the CAB2 strain revealed fragmented mitochondria at approximately 2 hr PGT.
source: The changes in morphology of the mitochondria also occurred during infection, as host cells invaded with the CAB2 strain revealed similar fragmented mitochondria at approximately 2 hr PGT (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification.

claim: Cells infected with CAB2Δvpa0226 strain exhibit normal mitochondrial morphology throughout the infection.
source: In addition, cells infected with CAB2Δvpa0226 strain exhibit normal mitochondrial morphology throughout the infection (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification.

claim: Mitochondrial fragmentation was dependent on the intact catalytic activity of VPA0226.
source: Consistent with the transfection studies, mitochondrial fragmentation was dependent on the intact catalytic activity of VPA0226 (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification.

claim: VPA0226 must be supplied intracellularly to cause changes in the mitochondria.
source: As we only saw changes in mitochondria when VPA0226 is provided by an intracellular source (invaded or transfected cells), we conclude that VPA0226 must be supplied intracellularly to cause changes in the mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on observations from both transfection and infection experiments.

claim: Cytochrome C is released into the cytosol in CAB2 and CAB2Δvpa0226+WT-infected cells, but not CAB2Δvpa0226 and CAB2Δvpa0226+S/A-infected cells by 5 hr PGT.
source: Consistent with this idea, we observed the release of Cytochrome C into the cytosol in CAB2 and CAB2Δvpa0226+WT-infected cells, but not CAB2Δvpa0226 and CAB2Δvpa0226+S/A-infected cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B) by 5 hr PGT.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification.

claim: Positive TUNEL staining is observed in CAB2 and CAB2Δvpa0226+WT infected cells but not in CAB2Δvpa0226 and CAB2Δvpa0226+S/A infected cells after 5 hr PGT.
source: Indeed, we observed positive TUNEL staining in CAB2 and CAB2Δvpa0226+WT infected cells but not in CAB2Δvpa0226 and CAB2Δvpa0226+S/A infected cells after 5 hr PGT (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification.

claim: Treatment of cells with Z-VAD-FMK did not alter the progression of V. parahaemolyticus-mediated invasion or the survival and escape of the CAB2 strains from the host cells.
source: Interestingly, while treatment of cells with an inhibitor of apoptosis Z-VAD-FMK did inhibit apoptosis in staurosporine-treated cells, Z-VAD-FMK did not alter the progression of V. parahaemolyticus-mediated invasion or the survival and escape of the CAB2 strains from the host cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by gentamicin protection assay data.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus escapes from the host cell 5 hr PGT whether or not apoptotic processes are active or inhibited.
source: However, death by apoptosis is not a mechanism used for cell lysis because V. parahaemolyticus escapes from the host cell 5 hr PGT whether or not apoptotic processes are active or inhibited (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on Z-VAD-FMK treatment experiments.

claim: Lipases similar to VPA0226 can esterify cholesterol by the transfer of an acyl group from an acyl-containing lipid to cholesterol thereby converting free cholesterol to a cholesteryl ester.
source: Previously, it was shown that lipases similar to VPA0226 can esterify cholesterol by the transfer of an acyl group from an acyl-containing lipid to cholesterol thereby converting free cholesterol to a cholesteryl ester (Buckley, 1982; Nawabi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Buckley, 1982 and Nawabi et al., 2008.

claim: Only the lipase activity, but not the transferase activity, has been observed previously for Vibrio lipases.
source: It should be noted that only the lipase activity, but not the transferase activity, has been observed previously for Vibrio lipases (Shinoda et al., 1991; Van der Henst et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Shinoda et al., 1991 and Van der Henst et al., 2018.

claim: Purified wildtype VPA0226 but not the catalytically inactive VPA0226-S/A mutant resulted in a concentration-dependent increase in fluorescence from a PLA2-specific fluorogenic substrate.
source: Purified wildtype VPA0226 but not the catalytically inactive VPA0226- S/A mutant resulted in a concentration-dependent increase in fluorescence from a PLA2-specific fluorogenic substrate (BODIPY PC-A2) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by fluorescence assay data.

claim: The wildtype but not the catalytically inactive VPA0226-S/A mutant facilitated the esterification of cholesterol in liposome assays.
source: We observed that the wildtype but not the catalytically inactive VPA0226-S/A mutant facilitated the esterification of cholesterol (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by thin layer chromatography data.

claim: The cholesteryl esters that dramatically changed in the presence of wildtype VPA0226 included CE(20:3), CE(20:4), CE(20:5) and CE(22:6).
source: Rather, the cholesteryl esters that did dramatically change in the presence of wildtype VPA0226 included CE(20:3), CE(20:4), CE(20:5) and CE(22:6) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by lipidomic analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Arachidonic acid (20:4) is implicated with innate immune signaling.
source: Interestingly, these fatty acids are ones implicated with innate immune signaling, with the most notable being arachidonic acid (20:4) (Tallima and El Ridi, 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Tallima and El Ridi, 2018.

claim: Depletion of cholesterol levels in cells lead to decrease in monolayer transepithelial electrical resistance and a significant increase in the paracellular permeability.
source: As shown previously, depletion of cholesterol levels in cells lead to decrease in monolayer transepithelial electrical resistance and a significant increase in the paracellular permeability (Lambert et al., 2005; Grunze and Deuticke, 1974).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Lambert et al., 2005 and Grunze and Deuticke, 1974.

claim: All three genes, HMGCR, HMGCS and DHCR24, were upregulated in cells expressing VPA0226, but not in cells with the empty vector or the catalytically inactive VPA0226H/A.
source: Using qPCR, we observed all three genes, HMGCR, HMGCS and DHCR24, were upregulated in cells expressing VPA0226, but not in cells with the empty vector or the catalytically inactive VPA0226H/A (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The plasma membrane fractions isolated from HeLa cells expressing VPA0226 had a statistically significant reduction in free cholesterol content compared to cells expressing either empty vector or catalytically inactive VPA0226.
source: Further, the plasma membrane fractions isolated from HeLa cells expressing VPA0226 had a statistically significant reduction in free cholesterol content compared to cells expressing either empty vector or catalytically inactive VPA0226 (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cholesterol quantification data.

claim: Cells expressing VPA0226, but not cells with the empty vector or the catalytically inactive VPA0226-H/A, lysed more readily when subjected to hypotonic stress.
source: We observed that cells expressing VPA0226, but not in cells with the empty vector or the catalytically inactive VPA0226-H/A, lysed more readily as indicated by an increase in fluorescence (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by propidium iodide binding assay data.

claim: Cells infected with either CAB2 or CAB2Δvpa0226+WT, but not with CAB2Δvpa0226 and CAB2Δvpa0226+S/A, take up the Sytox stain at 5 hr PGT, indicating that their membranes have been compromised.
source: We observed that cells infected with either CAB2 or CAB2Δvpa0226+WT, but not with CAB2Δvpa0226 and CAB2Δvpa0226+S/A, take up the Sytox stain at 5 hr PGT, indicating that their membranes have been compromised (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification.

claim: Only cells that are invaded with CAB2 take up the Sytox stain.
source: Furthermore, only cells that are invaded with CAB2 take up the Sytox stain, consistent with the observation that only the invaded cells with an internal source of VPA0226 have compromised membranes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by confocal microscopy images.

claim: CAB2 was no longer able to efficiently egress from cholesterol-treated cells at 7 hr PGT.
source: We discovered that CAB2 was no longer able to efficiently egress from cholesterol-treated cells at 7 hr PGT and there was no change in the inability of CAB2Δvpa0226 to egress from host cells (Figure 5F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by gentamicin protection assay data with cholesterol treatment.

claim: CAB2Δvpa0226 could escape from host cells at 7 hr PGT when treated with HPCD.
source: We then treated CAB2 and CAB2Δvpa0226 infected cells with hydroxypropyl β-cyclodextrin (HPCD), a compound that depletes cholesterol from membranes (Chakrabarti et al., 2017). We observed that CAB2Δvpa0226 could now escape from host cells at 7 hr PGT and that CAB2 followed an expected course for egress, albeit, somewhat accelerated (Figure 5F and H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by gentamicin protection assay data with HPCD treatment.

claim: Changes in free cholesterol are essential for egress of V. parahaemolyticus from host cells.
source: These studies support our model that changes in free cholesterol are essential for egress of V. parahaemolyticus from host cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on cholesterol manipulation experiments.

claim: The mechanism of entry for V. parahaemolyticus was discovered to be mediated by the deamidase activity of VopC.
source: Previously, the mechanism of entry for V. parahaemolyticus was discovered to be mediated by the deamidase activity of VopC (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: The escape route for V. parahaemolyticus mediated host cell invasion is dependent on the Type two secreted lipase VPA0226.
source: Herein, we find that the escape route for V. parahaemolyticus mediated host cell invasion is dependent on the Type two secreted lipase VPA0226, which compromises the integrity of the plasma membrane by using polyunsaturated fatty acids to esterify cholesterol in the infected cell.
evidence: This is stated as a primary conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: VPA0226 compromises the integrity of the plasma membrane by using polyunsaturated fatty acids to esterify cholesterol in the infected cell.
source: Herein, we find that the escape route for V. parahaemolyticus mediated host cell invasion is dependent on the Type two secreted lipase VPA0226, which compromises the integrity of the plasma membrane by using polyunsaturated fatty acids to esterify cholesterol in the infected cell.
evidence: This is stated as a primary conclusion in the Discussion section.

claim: VPA0226 provides an essential activity for the virulence of the T3SS2 pathogenicity island by providing a convenient mechanism for escape.
source: For this pathogen, VPA0226 provides an essential activity for the virulence of the T3SS2 pathogenicity island by providing a convenient mechanism for escape.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus uses many tools outside of the T3SS2 pathogenicity island for a successful infection.
source: These findings make it very clear that, although we attribute V. parahaemolyticus virulence to T3SS2 (11,43), this bacterial pathogen uses many tools outside of this pathogenicity island for a successful infection.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: VPA0226 appears to be constitutively secreted from V. parahaemolyticus by the type two secretion system.
source: VPA0226 appears to be constitutively secreted from V. parahaemolyticus by the type two secretion system, as we saw no accumulation of VPA0226 inside V. parahaemolyticus cells, indicating that, as it is synthesized it is secreted (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on Western blot data.

claim: VPA0226 is constitutively secreted by intracellular bacteria during infection.
source: We propose that VPA0226 is constitutively secreted by intracellular bacteria during infection because we only observe changes in the mitochondria, release of cytochrome C, TUNEL-positive cells and Sytox membrane permeability in host cells that are invaded with V. parahaemolyticus expressing wild-type VPA0226.
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on multiple observations.

claim: VPA0226 targets host cell machinery from within the host cell and not from the outside.
source: Therefore, VPA0226 targets host cell machinery from within the host cell and not from the outside.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on observations that only invaded cells show VPA0226 effects.

claim: How and why VPA0226 localizes specifically to the mitochondria is unclear.
source: As VPA0226 does not appear to encode a mitochondrial localization domain, how and why it localizes specifically to the mitochondria is unclear.
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of uncertainty.

claim: Homologues of VPA0226 in Vibrio species such as vhhA in V. harveyi, VvPlpA in V. vulnificus, and phlA in V. mimicus, are implicated in virulence but have only been shown to possess the lipase activity.
source: Homologues of VPA0226 in Vibrio species such as vhhA in V. harveyi, VvPlpA in V. vulnificus, and phlA in V. mimicus, are implicated in virulence but have only been shown to possess the lipase activity (Zhong et al., 2006; Jang et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Zhong et al., 2006; Jang et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2002.

claim: Recombinant VvhA from Vibrio vulnificus was shown to induce NF-κB-dependent mitochondrial cell death mediated by the production of lipid raft-dependent ROS.
source: Recombinant VvhA from Vibrio vulnificus was shown to induce NF-κB-dependent mitochondrial cell death mediated by the production of lipid raft-dependent ROS (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: lec/VC_A0218 in V. cholerae with lipase activity is implicated in escape from the infected amoeba.
source: Another structural homologue lec/VC_A0218 in V. cholerae with lipase activity is implicated in escape from the infected amoeba (Van der Henst et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Van der Henst et al., 2018.

claim: TgLCAT, lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase encoded by Toxoplasma gondii is implicated in host cell egress.
source: In addition, a genetically non-homologous but functionally similar TgLCAT, lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase encoded by a protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii is also implicated in host cell egress (Pszenny et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Pszenny et al., 2016.

claim: VPA0226 is in a clan of enzymes containing invariant catalytic Ser, Gly, Asn and His residues which are referred to as GDSL-like lipases.
source: Using bioinformatics and clustering analysis, we find that VPA0226 is in a clan of enzymes containing invariant catalytic Ser, Gly, Asn and His residues which are referred to as GDSL-like lipases (Akoh et al., 2004; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Akoh et al., 2004 and supported by sequence alignment.

claim: VPA0226 and homologs from other Vibrio species, together with the Salmonella phospholipase effector SseJ, are located in a mostly bacterial subfamily, closely related to plant and fungal GDSL lipases.
source: VPA0226 and homologs from other Vibrio species, together with the Salmonella phospholipase effector SseJ, are located in a mostly bacterial subfamily, closely related to plant and fungal GDSL lipases and only remotely related to animal GDSL lipases, for example human Phospholipase B1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by CLANS clustering analysis.

claim: The presence of VPA0226 in the V. parahaemolyticus genome predated the acquisition of the T3SS2 pathogenicity island.
source: Based on this conservation, we predict that the presence of VPA0226 in the V. parahaemolyticus genome predated the acquisition of the T3SS2 pathogenicity island (Makino et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on phylogenetic analysis and cited to Makino et al., 2003.

claim: VPA0226 appears to act like a phospholipase A2 (PLA2) because it specifically transfers an acyl group from position two from the glycerol backbone of a phospholipid to cholesterol.
source: Interestingly, VPA0226 appears to act like a phospholipase A2 (PLA2) because, using lipidomics, we observe that VPA0226 specifically transfers an acyl group from position two from the glycerol backbone of a phospholipid to cholesterol (Haas and Stanley, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation based on lipidomic data and cited to Haas and Stanley, 2007.

claim: The products from the VPA0226 reaction are esterified cholesterol and lysophospholipids, both of which destabilize membranes.
source: The products from this reaction are esterified cholesterol and lysophospholipids, both of which destabilize membranes (Aikawa et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Aikawa et al., 2015.

claim: The esterified cholesterol produced by VPA0226 are quite selective PUFAs, including 20:3, 20:4 (arachidonic acid) and 20:5 and 22:6 (fish oil lipids).
source: The esterified cholesterol produced by VPA0226 are quite selective PUFAs, including 20:3, 20:4 (arachidonic acid) and 20:5 and 22:6 (fish oil lipids).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of lipidomic findings.

claim: L. monocytogenes and Shigella flexneri manipulate the accessible pool of cholesterol for infection.
source: Recently, it has been reported that L. monocytogenes and Shigella flexneri, manipulate the accessible pool of cholesterol for infection and that acute mobilization of this plasma membrane cholesterol pool by oxysterols confers immunity (Abrams et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Abrams et al., 2020.

claim: Acute mobilization of plasma membrane cholesterol pool by oxysterols confers immunity against L. monocytogenes and Shigella flexneri.
source: Recently, it has been reported that L. monocytogenes and Shigella flexneri, manipulate the accessible pool of cholesterol for infection and that acute mobilization of this plasma membrane cholesterol pool by oxysterols confers immunity (Abrams et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Abrams et al., 2020.

claim: After V. parahaemolyticus escapes from the endosome, VPA0226 is secreted into the host cytosol, localizes to the mitochondria and esterifies cholesterol over the course of about 5–6 hr.
source: After V. parahaemolyticus escapes from the endosome, we postulate VPA0226 is secreted into the host cytosol, localizes to the mitochondria and esterifies cholesterol over the course of about 5–6 hr.
evidence: This is stated as a postulate based on the temporal sequence of observed events.

claim: During infection, V. parahaemolyticus reaches a density of about 300 bacteria/invaded cell.
source: During that time, V. parahaemolyticus reaches a density of about 300 bacteria/invaded cell and, due to mechanical stress (or possibly another unknown factor) egresses from the host cell.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from infection experiments.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus egresses from the host cell due to mechanical stress or possibly another unknown factor.
source: During that time, V. parahaemolyticus reaches a density of about 300 bacteria/invaded cell and, due to mechanical stress (or possibly another unknown factor) egresses from the host cell.
evidence: This is stated with speculation about the trigger for egress.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus uniquely utilizes two independent secretion systems to support its intracellular lifestyle.
source: We observe that V. parahaemolyticus uniquely utilizes two independent secretion systems to support its intracellular lifestyle.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the findings that T3SS2 mediates invasion and T2SS secretes VPA0226 for egress.

claim: V. parahaemolyticus appears to have utilized existing resources to evolve an efficient mechanism for invasion, propagation and escape.
source: From the perspective of virulence, V. parahaemolyticus appears to have utilized existing resources to evolve an efficient mechanism for invasion, propagation and escape.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the evolutionary significance of the findings.

claim: There is more interplay between secretion systems, providing unique, synergistic mechanisms to support a successful lifestyle of possibly pathogenicity, symbiosis and/or parasitosis.
source: We speculate, considering the time pathogens have to evolve, that there is actually more interplay between secretion systems, providing unique, synergistic mechanisms to support a successful lifestyle of possibly pathogenicity, symbiosis and/or parasitosis.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about broader implications.
